paper_title: Out of Sight, Still in Mind: Token Compression for Omni-LLMs

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: The goal of this paper is to reduce the input token cost of Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) at inference time. Omni-LLMs reason jointly over audio, video and text, but the cost of the three streams is highly unbalanced: visual tokens account for the vast majority of the input, and are highly redundant. In this paper, we propose ReMo, a training-free framework that compresses visual tokens by redistributing their information across modalities: a visual token is kept only if its information appears nowhere else. ReMo achieves this in two ways: (i) it aligns audio and video in a shared space via closed-form calibration, and removes visual tokens already explained by the audio or by other visual tokens; and (ii) it replaces object-level visual tokens, identified by a lightweight object detector, with compact text proxies, short descriptions of each object and its location, conveying the same content in far fewer tokens. On Qwen2.5-Omni at two model scales, ReMo removes 54% of the input tokens with comparable accuracy. It performs comparably to the full-token model, reaching 101.2% and 101.4% of its average accuracy over five audio-visual benchmarks.

sections.content: The goal of this paper is to reduce the input token cost of Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) at inference time. Omni-LLMs reason jointly over audio, video and text, but the cost of the three streams is highly unbalanced: visual tokens account for the vast majority of the input, and are highly redundant. In this paper, we propose ReMo, training-free framework that compresses visual tokens by redistributing their information across modalities: visual token is kept only if its information appears nowhere else. ReMo achieves this in two ways: (i) it aligns audio and video in shared space via closed-form calibration, and removes visual tokens already explained by the audio or by other visual tokens; and (ii) it replaces object-level visual tokens, identified by lightweight object detector, with compact text proxies, short descriptions of each object and its location, conveying the same content in far fewer tokens. On Qwen2.5-Omni at two model scales, ReMo removes 54% of the input tokens with comparable accuracy. It performs comparably to the full-token model, reaching 101.2% and 101.4% of its average accuracy over five audio-visual benchmarks. 1. Introduction Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) extend LLMs to perceive audio, vision and text jointly, achieving strong results on real-world audio-visual understanding [20, 40, 44, 48, 49]. This capability comes at cost: encoding all three modalities inflates the input sequence to tens of thousands of tokens, most of which come from the visual stream. At this length, the quadratic cost of attention becomes the primary bottleneck for both latency and memory. Reducing the token count without sacrificing accuracy is therefore central to deploying Omni-LLMs at scale. Token compression tailored to Omni-LLMs has only recently emerged, aiming to reduce the large number of audio or visual input tokens before decoding [22, 33]. Rather than treating each modality in isolation, these methods exploit cross-modal relationships, such as audio-visual similarity or the relevance of audio and visual tokens to the text query, to identify redundant or less relevant input tokens for pruning. Cross-modal cues guide token pruning by distinguishing complementary Figure 1. Cross-modal redistribution. large fraction of visual tokens in an Omni-LLM are redundant. Our method projects audio and video into common space to drop redundant visual tokens, then replaces the discarded object semantics with compact text proxies, redistributing visual information across the audio and text streams. Existing approaches broadly fall information from content already captured by another modality. into two categories depending on whether they require training. Training-based methods, such as OmniSIFT [11], EchoingPixels [15] and ContextGuard [23], learn dedicated compression component; whilst effective, they must be retrained for each backbone, limiting their applicability. Training-free methods avoid this cost. DASH [28] uses audio boundaries to select informative video frames and adaptively allocate the compression budget. OmniZip [41] instead explicitly considers cross-modal redundancy, estimating it from the cosine similarity of raw modality embeddings; however, this assumes the two modalities are comparable in their native spaces, when in fact their embeddings are poorly aligned [19, 25, 31, 55]. OmniScope [39] and OmniSelect [50] address this issue by using external pretrained encoders to estimate multimodal relevance, introducing an additional expensive module outside the Omni-LLM. In this paper, we revisit how the multimodal capabilities of Omni-LLMs can be used for token compression without fine-tuning. Building on prior use of audio to represent visual semantics, we introduce text as complementary compression modality, reducing the visual tokens that dominate the input sequence, as illustrated in Fig. 1. First, ReMo removes only visual tokens whose content is already captured by the accompanying audio, without heavy external modules or gradient updates. Second, pruning visual tokens can discard object-level semantics that are easily expressed in language. We therefore use lightweight object detector to identify such semantics and insert the detected object names as compact text proxies into the multimodal input. In this way, few text 1 tokens can preserve information that would otherwise require many visual tokens, while the remaining visual tokens retain information that cannot be supplied by the other modalities. Each route poses its own challenge. For the first, deciding whether an audio token and visual token describe the same concept is difficult, because their embeddings live in poorly aligned spaces. We therefore project both modalities into common space using closed-form calibration step, where their agreement can be measured directly. For the second, the inserted words must not float free of the scene. We place each description according to the spatial position of the object it replaces, so the text stays anchored to where its content appears. The result, ReMo, offloads high-level visual semantics onto the audio and text streams, while reserving visual tokens for complementary visual detail. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that this redistribution works in practice. controlled audio-to-video retrieval analysis first verifies the projection at the heart of ReMo, improving R@1 from 2.7 to 31.3 over raw embeddings and confirming that audio and video are aligned reliably enough to ground our cross-modal saliency. We then evaluate ReMo on Qwen2.5-Omni [48] across four audio-visual understanding benchmarks and one captioning benchmark. At compression rate comparable to the strongest training-free baseline, ReMo largely preserves accuracy and performs comparably to the fulltoken model, reaching 101.2% and 101.4% of its average accuracy at the 3B and 7B model sizes. Consistent gains at both sizes, across benchmarks of different natures, and without fine-tuning, suggest that using both audio and text to preserve visual semantics is an effective strategy for compressing Omni-LLM inputs. 2. Related Work Omni-modal LLMs. Building on multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), recent line of work extends vision-language models to jointly process text, image, audio, and video within single LLM, often referred to as Omni-LLMs. Proprietary systems such as GPT-4o [20] and Gemini [8, 43] show strong audio-visual reasoning, and growing body of open models follows [5, 9, 12, 30, 40, 48]. These models pair modality-specific encoders with shared LLM decoder, project each modality into common embedding space, and interleave the resulting tokens into chunk-structured sequences. complementary line of work improves these models at inference time through decoding interventions [7, 21, 24, 54]. However, such methods change how existing tokens are read while leaving the token budget untouched, so the quadratic cost of attention over thousands of multimodal tokens remains the main bottleneck. Token compression for Omni-LLMs. Token compression reduces this cost by shrinking the decoders input sequence. For general multimodal LLMs, methods compress the visual stream by pruning low-attention tokens after an early layer [3], fitting the attention distribution [53], merging similar tokens [1], or selecting dominant ones [51], without considering audio. Recent Omni-LLM compression methods fall into two groups. Training-free methods include FastAV [22] and OmniDrop [33], which prune progressively inside the decoder using attention, and OmniZip [41], DASH [28], OmniScope [39], and OmniSelect [50], which prune audio-visual tokens at the input level. Training-based methods include OmniSIFT [11] and EchoingPixels [15], which learn dedicated compression modules, and ContextGuard [23], which learns predictor of audio-explainable visual semantics. ReMo performs training-free, input-level compression. While most methods compress both streams, ContextGuard preserves audio and prunes audio-explainable visual ReMo extends this principle to text, injecting compact proxies to preserve object-level visual semantics while retaining all audio tokens. tokens. The modality gap in multimodal models. Embeddings from different modalities rarely share common geometry. Even when encoders are trained to align them, they occupy separate regions of the representation space, phenomenon characterized as the modality gap [31] and linked to conical structure in the embedding space. The gap is not specific to one modality pair: it has been reported across image, video, audio, and 3D data [19], and traced to modality-specific components separable from the shared bimodal signal [10]. growing line of work seeks to reduce it, either through learned alignment objectives [16, 25] or by exploiting the geometry of the gap to transfer across modalities without paired supervision [19]. This gap has direct consequences for input-level compression in Omni-LLMs, where audio-video redundancy must be judged before the decoder. OmniZip [41] scores this redundancy from raw-embedding cosine similarity, which is directly exposed to the gap. ContextGuard [23] instead trains an audio-to-video prediction module to bridge the two spaces, while OmniScope [39] and OmniSelect [50] rely on pretrained CLIP [36] and AudioCLIP [17] encoders, respectively. OmniDrop [33] sidesteps the problem entirely by pruning in intermediate decoder layers rather than at the input. In contrast, ReMo uses simple closed-form calibration to align the two modalities, requiring no gradients or optimizer. Bridging vision and text tokens. complementary line connects visual content with the text token space. ReVisiT [6] shows that vision tokens intrinsically encode object-level semantics that surface when projected into the text vocabulary, indicating that much of their content is recoverable in language form. ViKey [27] overlays frame-index prompts on sampled frames and maps query keywords to those indices, using text cues as temporal anchors for sparsely sampled video. In the reverse direction, VIST [47] renders text into images and compresses the rendered features into few visual tokens, exploiting the spatial redundancy of text. Together these results suggest that object-level semantics transfer between the two token types. In this paper, we exploit this property by replacing redundant visual tokens with compact, spatially grounded text proxies rather than simply discarding them. 2 Figure 2. Overview of ReMo. We evaluate on four audio-visual understanding benchmarks, WorldSense [18] (World.), DailyOmni [56] (Daily.), Video-MME [13] (MME), and OmniVideoBench [29] (OmniVid.), and one captioning benchmark, video-SALMONN2 test set [40] (video-SAL2.). We report per-benchmark accuracy and an aggregate Avg. that normalizes each benchmark so the full-token model scores 100 and averages across benchmarks. We further evaluate ReMo on Video-MME Long [13] and LVOmniBench [42] for long-video understanding, and StreamingBench [32], FutureOmni [4], and OmniMMI [46] for streaming evaluation, with results reported in Tab. 6. On the 3B backbone, ReMo retains near full-token performance despite removing 54% of the input, reaching 100.5% and 99.3% average accuracy in the long-video and streaming settings, respectively. On 7B, it performs comparably to the full-token model in both settings, reaching 101.3% and 102.4%. These results show that ReMo remains effective beyond the short-video setting used in Tab. 1. Due to GPU memory constraints, experiments are run on four NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs; benchmark and implementation details are provided in Sec. of the supp. mat. Text proxies help only when information is lost. Tab. 7 tests when the text proxies actually help. Added on top of the full video set, they leave accuracy essentially unchanged, since the information they carry is already present, so the proxies neither help nor hurt. The picture changes once tokens are pruned. Added on top of random 50% prune, the same proxies recover much of the lost accuracy (+2.5 and +3.6 on World. and Daily.), because they reintroduce semantics the pruning had discarded. Text proxies are thus useful precisely when information has been removed, not as generic add-on. Under pruning, placing the proxies at their spatial position (t,h,w) works better than (t,t,t). We test this in Tab. 8. Rather than adding text proxies, we revive the same number of discarded video tokens (Nadd, the average number of text tokens ReMo adds) from within detected regions, choosing them either at random or by our saliency score (Eq. (8)). This matches the detected regions and the token budget across all variants, so the only difference is whether the object is expressed as few words or as its original video tokens. Both revival rules fall below ReMo on both benchmarks, reaching 47.2 and 47.3 on World. and 57.2 and 57.3 on Daily., whereas ReMo reaches 47.8 and 58.3. Naming an object in few words is thus not only cheaper than storing its pixels but also more effective, since the proxy states the semantics directly while the revived tokens still carry redundant appearance detail. Who uses the text proxies? Tab. 9 examines which token types benefit from access to the injected text proxies. Allowing all tokens to attend to the proxies performs best on both benchmarks. Restricting access to only audio-visual tokens reduces performance by 0.6/1.0 points on World./Daily., while allowing only text tokens causes drops of 0.7/0.4. Removing 7 Figure 4. These results suggest that the injected semantics are not used by single token type, but serve as shared context that benefits both modality and text representations. Additional analysis of attention to the text proxies is provided in Sec. E.3 of supp. mat. Object sources for text proxies. Tab. 10 compares full-caption and object-level semantics. We denote objects from visual and audio captions as Cv and Ca, and detector outputs as Y; intersections retain detected objects, while set differences exclude them. Full-caption injection performs worse, likely because long caption sequences disrupt the interleaved audio-visual structure seen during training. Excluding objects from our detector consistently reduces accuracy on both benchmarks, whereas retaining their intersection yields comparable performance. Candidates from Qwen3.8-27B [34] and Audio-Flamingo-Next-Instruct [14] perform comparably to our lightweight detector but require much larger auxiliary models, favoring the detectors balance of accuracy and efficiency. See Sec. of supp. mat. for details. Hyperparameter sensitivity. Fig. 4 varies each hyperparameter in turn. The selection budget ρav trades accuracy for compression as expected: keeping more video tokens raises accuracy but lowers the compression rate, so we set ρav=0.4 to match the compression of the training-free baselines rather than to maximize accuracy. The local detail budget ρl peaks around 0.05, where restoring few high-detail tokens helps before extra tokens start to add redundancy. The temporal-merging threshold τ is broadly flat, with mild peak near 0.05, showing that ReMo is not sensitive to its exact value. For the number of canonical directions K, both retrieval and accuracy saturate by 256 and stay flat beyond it. Overall, performance stays within Figure 5. Extreme compression ratios. Accuracy under increasingly aggressive token compression on the 3B and 7B backbones, measured on Daily. ReMo degrades more gracefully than competing methods and maintains the strongest performance from 65% to 90% compression. narrow band across these settings, with mild peaks, which our defaults are set to. Performance under extreme compression. Fig. 5 evaluates robustness under increasingly aggressive compression. ReMo degrades gracefully as the compression rate increases and remains above all competing methods across both model scales. At the most aggressive ratios, OmniZip and OmniSelect even fall below random pruning, showing that they struggle under extreme compression. In contrast, at 90% compression, ReMo still achieves 51.3% accuracy on 3B and 52.2% on 7B, substantially narrowing the gap to the full-token model. This shows that ReMo remains effective even under extreme compression. Hyperparameter settings for each baseline and compression ratio are provided in Sec. of supp. mat. 6. Conclusion We presented ReMo, training-free token compression framework for Omni-LLMs. ReMo removes visual tokens whose information is already captured by audio through common-space projection and preserves object-level semantics through compact text proxies with spatially grounded positions. On Qwen2.5-Omni at two scales and Qwen3-Omni-30B, ReMo compresses over half of the input tokens while performing comparably to the full-token model and reducing memory and latency. ReMo also remains effective on long-video and streaming benchmarks and degrades gracefully under extreme compression. These results suggest that cross-modal redistribution preserves multimodal information with fewer tokens, enabling efficient processing of longer, richer inputs. Despite our improvements, compression needs vary across tasks and inputs, making adaptive compression natural direction for future work.

Audio-Visual Preprocessing The Qwen2.5-Omni [48] preprocessing implementation used in our setup truncates audio to five minutes1. Video frames are sampled at 2 FPS by default, with maximum of 768 frames2. When this limit is exceeded, frames are sampled uniformly across the input span at lower effective frame rate. Caption Generation and Injection We evaluate visual and audio captions as alternatives to the object text extracted by YOLO [52] in ReMo. We use Qwen3.8-27B [34] for visual captioning and Audio-FlamingoNext-Instruct [14] for audio captioning. H.1. Visual Caption Generation For each temporal patch containing two frames, we caption the first frame using the frame indices stored in the YOLO cache. Qwen3.8-27B receives single image and the following prompt. Describe the visible objects and actions in this image in one or two sentences. We do not provide downstream questions, answer choices, ground truth answers, or YOLO labels during caption generation. Frame indices and captions are cached for each video and reused across questions associated with the same video. H.2. Audio Caption Generation We generate audio captions using Audio-Flamingo-NextInstruct with the following prompt: Describe the audible sounds and their sources in one or two sentences. H.3. Proxy Injection We replace the object text extracted by YOLO with the generated captions, injecting all caption subword embeddings in their original order without pooling or truncation. Reported compression rates include all injected caption tokens (Tab. 10). H.4. Object Separation To separate entities mentioned in captions according to YOLO detections, we append follow-up prompt to the same conversation after caption generation. For visual captions, Qwen3.8-27B receives: YOLO detected: {objects} List the visible physical objects mentioned in your caption: "yolo" for matches to YOLO (including synonyms; use YOLO labels), "caption" for the rest. Return only JSON: {"yolo": [], "caption": []}. For audio captions, Audio-Flamingo-Next-Instruct receives: YOLO detected: {objects} List the physical sound sources described in your caption: "yolo" for matches to YOLO (including synonyms; use YOLO labels), "caption" for the rest.
